tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Management – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: Management is best described as the process of:
options: Planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling resources to achieve organisational goals efficiently and effectively
questions.explanation: It coordinates human, financial, physical and informational resources.

questions.question_text: Mary Parker Follett defined management as:
options: The art of getting things done through people
Knowing exactly what you want men to do
questions.explanation: Her definition stresses working through people.

questions.question_text: "To manage is to forecast and plan, to organise, to command, to coordinate and to control" is the definition of:
questions.explanation: Fayol gave five elements of management.

questions.question_text: Koontz defined management as the art of getting things done:
options: Through and with people in formally organised groups
questions.explanation: The key phrase is "through and with people in formally organised groups".

questions.question_text: The three views of management are as a:
options: Process, a discipline and a group of people
questions.explanation: Management can be seen as functions, a field of study and the managers themselves.

questions.question_text: The "5 Ms" of resources managed by management are:
options: Men, money, materials, machines and methods
questions.explanation: Time and markets are added in some lists.

questions.question_text: Administration differs from management in that administration is mainly:
options: An execution function of lower levels
A top-level function concerned with determining objectives and broad policies
questions.explanation: Management executes the policies; today the terms are often used interchangeably.

questions.question_text: Which is a characteristic of management?
options: It is goal-oriented, universal and a continuous process
It is applicable to business only
questions.explanation: It is also multi-dimensional, dynamic, an intangible force and a group activity.

questions.question_text: Management is called a science because it has:
options: A systematic body of knowledge with principles based on experiments, though not as exact as pure sciences
questions.explanation: It is a "soft" or inexact science.

questions.question_text: Management is called an art because it involves:
options: Application of knowledge through personal skill, creativity and practice
questions.explanation: Leadership skill is individual and improves with experience.

questions.question_text: Management is regarded as an emerging profession because it:
options: Has specialised knowledge and representative bodies but lacks restricted entry and a legally enforced code
questions.explanation: AIMA and AMA are representative bodies.

questions.question_text: Management is called a "soft science" because:
options: Its principles deal with human behaviour and are flexible, not exact
questions.explanation: Behaviour cannot be predicted with certainty.

questions.question_text: Which is an objective of management?
options: Achieving organisational, social and personal objectives
questions.explanation: It balances the objectives of various stakeholders.

questions.question_text: Which shows the importance of management?
options: It removes the need for staff
It achieves group goals, increases efficiency and creates a dynamic organisation
questions.explanation: Management helps meet changing environments.

questions.question_text: Efficiency in management means:
options: Doing the task correctly, i.e., getting the maximum output from minimum input
questions.explanation: It is often described as "doing things right".

questions.question_text: Effectiveness in management means:
options: Achieving the goals set, i.e., doing the right things
questions.explanation: It is "doing the right things".

questions.question_text: Efficiency differs from effectiveness in that efficiency is concerned with:
options: Means (resource use), effectiveness with ends (goal achievement)
questions.explanation: Efficiency relates inputs to outputs.

questions.question_text: A manager must be both efficient and effective because:
options: Efficiency without effectiveness wastes resources on the wrong goals, and effectiveness without efficiency is costly
questions.explanation: Both are needed for success.

questions.question_text: An example of an efficient but ineffective manager is one who:
options: Produces goods at low cost that nobody wants
Produces goods people want at high cost
questions.explanation: Resources are used well but the goal is missed.

questions.question_text: Productivity is the:
questions.explanation: It measures how well resources are converted into output.

questions.question_text: The levels of management are:
questions.explanation: Each has distinct functions.

questions.question_text: The functions of top-level management include:
options: Setting objectives, formulating policies and overall strategy
questions.explanation: It is concerned with the overall direction of the organisation.

questions.question_text: The functions of middle-level management include:
options: Interpreting policies and coordinating between top and lower levels
questions.explanation: They translate top-level plans into departmental plans.

questions.question_text: The functions of lower-level management include:
options: Supervising workers, assigning tasks and ensuring day-to-day operations
questions.explanation: Foremen and supervisors work at this level.

questions.question_text: Compared with lower levels, the top-level manager spends more time on:
questions.explanation: Lower levels spend more time on direction and control.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Management – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: Katz identified which three managerial skills?
questions.explanation: The importance of each varies by level.

questions.question_text: Besides Katz's skills, an important skill today is:
questions.explanation: Others: analytical, digital and interpersonal skills.

questions.question_text: The functions of management include:
options: Planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling
questions.explanation: These form the management process.

questions.question_text: Fayol's functions of management are:
options: Planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling
questions.explanation: He gave five functions.

questions.question_text: Koontz and O'Donnell listed the functions as:
options: Planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling
questions.explanation: They added staffing as a separate function.

questions.question_text: POSDCORB was proposed by:
questions.explanation: It stands for Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Co-ordinating, Reporting, Budgeting.

questions.question_text: Coordination is called the essence of management because:
options: It is only for top managers
It integrates the efforts of individuals toward common objectives
questions.explanation: It runs through all functions.

questions.question_text: The functions of management are:
questions.explanation: Planning leads to organising, which leads to staffing, and so on.

questions.question_text: Henry Mintzberg is known for:
options: Studying what managers actually do and classifying managerial roles
questions.explanation: He described ten managerial roles.

questions.question_text: Mintzberg's three categories of roles are:
questions.explanation: There are ten roles in total.

questions.question_text: Which is an interpersonal role?
questions.explanation: They arise from the manager's authority.

questions.question_text: Which is an informational role?
questions.explanation: The manager receives and transmits information.

questions.question_text: Which is a decisional role?
options: Entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator and negotiator
questions.explanation: The manager makes significant choices.

questions.question_text: Mintzberg's study revealed that managers' work is:
options: Fragmented, brief and varied, not a neat set of orderly functions
questions.explanation: Managers face constant interruptions.

questions.question_text: The pre-classical contributors to management include:
options: Adam Smith, Robert Owen, Charles Babbage and Kautilya
questions.explanation: They came before the classical period.

questions.question_text: Adam Smith contributed to management through:
options: The principle of division of labour (pin factory example)
questions.explanation: He wrote The Wealth of Nations (1776).

questions.question_text: Robert Owen is known for:
options: Pioneering concern for workers' welfare and treating them as important resources
questions.explanation: He is often called the father of personnel management.

questions.question_text: Charles Babbage contributed:
options: The idea of division of mental labour and the analytical engine/computer concept
questions.explanation: He extended Smith's idea to mental work.

questions.question_text: Kautilya's contribution is:
options: His Arthashastra, a treatise on administration, statecraft and economic policy
questions.explanation: It shows early Indian thought on administration.

questions.question_text: The Industrial Revolution created a need for management because:
options: Factories needed coordination of large workforces and machines
questions.explanation: Large-scale production demanded organisation.

questions.question_text: The father of scientific management is:
questions.explanation: He developed the scientific approach to work.

questions.question_text: Taylor's two books are:
options: The Functions of the Executive and Industrial Management
Shop Management and The Principles of Scientific Management
The Human Problems of an Industrial Civilization
questions.explanation: Published in 1903 and 1911.

questions.question_text: Taylor's pig iron experiment at Bethlehem Steel showed that:
options: Scientific selection, training, rest pauses and incentives raised daily output sharply
questions.explanation: Output rose from about 12.5 to 47 tons per day.

questions.question_text: The principles of scientific management include:
options: Science not rule of thumb, harmony not discord, cooperation not individualism, maximum output
questions.explanation: He stressed development of each person to his greatest efficiency.

questions.question_text: The "mental revolution" means:
options: A change in the attitude of management and workers toward each other, from conflict to cooperation
questions.explanation: Both should focus on increasing the surplus.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Management – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: Which is a technique of scientific management?
options: Time study, motion study, fatigue study, standardisation and differential piece-rate
questions.explanation: Also functional foremanship.

questions.question_text: Time study is:
options: Determining the standard time to complete a job
questions.explanation: It sets a fair day's work.

questions.question_text: Motion study is:
options: Studying the movements in a job to eliminate wasteful ones
questions.explanation: It finds the one best way of doing a job.

questions.question_text: Fatigue study determines:
options: The amount and frequency of rest needed to overcome tiredness
questions.explanation: Rest pauses are scheduled.

questions.question_text: Standardisation means:
options: Setting standards for tools, materials, methods and working conditions
questions.explanation: It brings uniformity and efficiency.

questions.question_text: In the differential piece-rate system, a worker who produces:
options: Above the standard gets a higher rate per piece, and below the standard a lower rate
questions.explanation: It rewards efficient workers.

questions.question_text: Functional foremanship means:
options: Dividing the supervisor's work among eight specialists, four planning and four in the shop
questions.explanation: It violates unity of command.

questions.question_text: The Gilbreths are known for:
options: Motion study and the therblig (basic elements of motion)
questions.explanation: Frank and Lillian Gilbreth analysed motions.

questions.question_text: Henry Gantt contributed:
options: The Gantt chart and the task-and-bonus wage system
questions.explanation: He stressed scheduling and worker training.

questions.question_text: A Gantt chart is:
options: A bar chart showing planned and actual progress of work against time
questions.explanation: It is used in scheduling and control.

questions.question_text: Harrington Emerson contributed:
questions.explanation: He emphasised efficiency in industry.

questions.question_text: A criticism of scientific management is that it:
options: Treats workers as machines and ignores human and social needs
questions.explanation: Workers and unions resisted it.

questions.question_text: The significance of scientific management lies in:
options: Standardisation, scientific selection and training, and higher productivity
questions.explanation: It laid the foundation for modern management.

questions.question_text: The father of modern administrative management is:
questions.explanation: His focus was management at the top level.

questions.question_text: Fayol's book is:
questions.explanation: It was published in French in 1916.

questions.question_text: Fayol's six activities of an industrial enterprise are:
options: Buying, selling, storing, grading, transport, finance
Technical, commercial, financial, security, accounting and managerial
Planning, organising, directing, staffing, controlling, coordinating
questions.explanation: Managerial is the most important.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT one of Fayol's 14 principles?
questions.explanation: Mental revolution is Taylor's.

questions.question_text: Unity of command means:
options: Each employee receives orders from only one superior
One plan for a group of activities
questions.explanation: Unity of direction means one head and one plan for a group of activities with the same objective.

questions.question_text: The scalar chain is:
options: The chain of authority from top to bottom, and the gang plank is a direct link between peers to speed communication
questions.explanation: Fayol's "bridge" allows cross-communication.

questions.question_text: Centralisation means:
options: Concentration of decision-making authority at the top
questions.explanation: Decentralisation is the opposite.

questions.question_text: Taylor differs from Fayol in that Taylor focused on:
options: Top level, Fayol on the shop floor
Shop-floor (operational) efficiency, Fayol on top-level administration
questions.explanation: Taylor was an engineer; Fayol was an administrator.

questions.question_text: Gulick and Urwick contributed:
options: POSDCORB and the principles of administration
questions.explanation: They developed the administrative principles.

questions.question_text: Chester Barnard contributed:
options: The acceptance theory of authority and the concept of informal organisation
questions.explanation: His book was The Functions of the Executive (1938).

questions.question_text: The bureaucratic theory was propounded by:
questions.explanation: He was a German sociologist.

questions.question_text: Weber's three types of authority are:
questions.explanation: Bureaucracy rests on rational-legal authority.

tests.title: Unit 1: Introduction to Management – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: A feature of bureaucracy is:
options: Division of labour, hierarchy, rules and impersonal relations
questions.explanation: Also promotion on merit and written records.

questions.question_text: A merit of bureaucracy is _____, and a demerit is _____:
options: Predictability and fairness; rigidity and red tape
questions.explanation: Rules ensure consistency but can slow decisions.

questions.question_text: "Red tape" refers to:
options: Excessive rules and formalities that delay action
questions.explanation: It is a common criticism of bureaucracy.

questions.question_text: The human relations movement arose because:
options: Classical approaches ignored workers' social and psychological needs
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne studies highlighted these needs.

questions.question_text: The Hawthorne experiments were conducted by:
options: Elton Mayo and colleagues at the Western Electric Company
questions.explanation: They were conducted from 1924 to 1932.

questions.question_text: The Hawthorne effect is that:
options: Workers change behaviour when they know they are being observed or receive attention
questions.explanation: Productivity rose due to attention and social factors.

questions.question_text: A conclusion of the Hawthorne studies is:
options: Social and psychological factors and informal groups strongly affect productivity
questions.explanation: Workers are social beings.

questions.question_text: Mary Parker Follett contributed:
options: Her concepts of power with, constructive conflict and coordination (the "prophet of management")
questions.explanation: She stressed participation.

questions.question_text: The behavioural approach focuses on:
questions.explanation: It draws on psychology and sociology.

questions.question_text: Key contributors to the behavioural approach include:
questions.explanation: They studied motivation and leadership.

questions.question_text: A criticism of the human relations approach is that it:
options: Overemphasises human aspects and ignores the structure and technical side
questions.explanation: It was seen as too narrow.

questions.question_text: The quantitative approach to management uses:
options: Mathematical and statistical techniques for decision making
questions.explanation: Also called management science or operations research.

questions.question_text: Tools used in the quantitative approach include:
options: Linear programming, PERT/CPM, queuing and simulation
questions.explanation: They help in complex decisions.

questions.question_text: A limitation of the quantitative approach is that it:
options: Cannot easily deal with human and qualitative factors
questions.explanation: Models rely on assumptions.

questions.question_text: The systems approach views an organisation as:
options: A set of interrelated parts working together toward a common goal
questions.explanation: It considers the environment too.

questions.question_text: An open system differs from a closed system in that an open system:
questions.explanation: Business organisations are open systems.

questions.question_text: Synergy means:
options: The combined effect of parts working together is greater than the sum of their individual effects

questions.question_text: Subsystems are:
options: Smaller parts of a system, e.g., departments in an organisation
questions.explanation: They interact to form the whole.

questions.question_text: A merit of the systems approach is that it:
options: Gives a holistic view of the organisation and its environment
questions.explanation: A limitation is that it is abstract.

questions.question_text: The contingency approach states that:
options: There is no single best way of managing; the right approach depends on the situation
questions.explanation: It is also called the situational approach.

questions.question_text: Joan Woodward contributed to contingency theory by showing that:
options: Technology (unit, mass, process production) affects organisational structure
questions.explanation: Success depends on fit with technology.

questions.question_text: According to Burns and Stalker, mechanistic organisations suit _____ environments, and organic ones suit _____:
questions.explanation: Organic structures are flexible.

questions.question_text: Lawrence and Lorsch proposed that organisations need:
options: Differentiation and integration to fit their environment
questions.explanation: Different subunits must also be coordinated.

questions.question_text: A merit of the contingency approach is:
options: Flexibility and realism in matching management to the situation
questions.explanation: A demerit is that it lacks a universal theory.

questions.question_text: Which correctly compares the approaches?
options: Classical focuses on tasks and structure, behavioural on people, and modern on systems and situations
questions.explanation: They developed in that sequence.
